learnerStatement: Simulated learner. This review finds problems; it is not evidence that anyone learned.
learnerBoundary: Everyday numeracy, simple charts, comparing numbers and familiar household objects; no domain-specific theory assumed.

observations.prediction: Selected It falls and locked the take-home change prediction when pay rises from $19,000 to $21,000 under invented 10% and 30% marginal brackets.
observations.exploration: At $19,000 take-home was $17,100. Raised to $20,000: $18,000 take-home, up $900. Raised to $21,000: $18,700, up $1,600 overall. Raised again to $22,000: $19,400, showing the next $1,000 adds $700 after tax.
observations.reveal: The reveal corrected the answer to a $1,600 increase and explained only the $1,000 above $20,000 in the original scenario pays 30%. It stated the lower dollars retain their previous rate and disclosed invented brackets without credits or other taxes.
observations.visual: Inspected the inline dark 1257 by 936 screenshot at $21,000. A dashed threshold separated a large keep 90% region from a narrow above-threshold slice labelled 30% only here. Take-home, change and average tax were clearly displayed.
observations.isolation: No-history evaluation preview banner present. Visible trust count ignored.
observations.reference: Own CUA tab 543884163 snapshots and inspected inline screenshot; no screenshot file saved.

prediction.reason: The prompt directly tests the common all-income bracket interpretation.
prediction.evidence: Selected a fall in take-home before crossing the threshold.

interaction.reason: Incremental raises expose different marginal gains without a discontinuity.
interaction.evidence: The first $1,000 added $900 and each tested above-threshold $1,000 added $700.

payoff.reason: The reveal explains the preserved lower slice and accurate original comparison.
payoff.evidence: It quotes $17,100 to $18,700 and the $1,000 above the line.

clarity.reason: The threshold and slice labeling distinguish marginal from average taxation.
clarity.evidence: The screenshot labels 30% only here while average tax reads 11.0%.

transfer.reason: The reusable marginal principle is stated within the original tax model.
transfer.evidence: No different bracket structure or new application is worked.

accessibility.evidence: Keyboard, focus, contrast audit, phone, zoom/reflow and motion unknown.

surprise.reason: Entering a higher bracket changes the next slice rather than the whole paycheck.

visualExplanation.reason: The narrow extra slice makes the misconception visibly wrong.
visualExplanation.evidence: Most income remains in the keep 90% region.

playfulness.reason: Increment buttons make the boundary easy to probe.
playfulness.evidence: Three $1,000 raises reveal the change in marginal gain.

practicalValue.reason: It clarifies how marginal brackets work in the stated system.
practicalValue.evidence: The ending distinguishes the top rate from tax on all pay.

depth.reason: The lesson combines threshold behavior, marginal gain and average rate.
depth.evidence: At $21,000 the top rate is 30% while average tax is 11%.

complexity.reason: Dollar slices and incremental raises make a new marginal-rate distinction accessible.
complexity.conceptualDemand: Low to moderate: apply different percentages to different portions.
complexity.interfaceBurden: Low: slider and plus or minus $1,000 buttons.
complexity.conceptualChallenge: Crossing a threshold changes only the amount above it.
complexity.prerequisiteNovelty: Marginal versus average tax rate is the central new idea.
complexity.notationRepresentationBurden: Low: dollar readouts and a split rectangle.

whyCool: A feared tax cliff becomes a visible bend in how much of the next dollar is kept.
caveat: These invented brackets omit credits, other taxes and benefit interactions; the conclusion is limited to this system.
missingEvidence: No alternate bracket or benefit system was tested.
